summary.text: Longshore drift is the movement of sediment such as sand, pebbles and shells along a coast, parallel to the shoreline, carried by a current within the surf zone.
When wind arrives at an angle it squeezes water along the coast into a current, so the drift depends on the angle at which waves come in.
On the beach, swash carries sand up at a slant and backwash drains it straight down, so sand zigzags along the shore many tens of meters a day.

items.prompt: You drop a bright red pebble on a beach where waves rush up at a slant and the water then drains straight back down the slope. Where is the pebble after a day?

options.label: Further along the beach, after a zigzag path
In the same spot, just moved up and down
Carried straight out to deeper water
Buried exactly where it was dropped

items.explain: Swash pushes sand up at an angle and backwash pulls it straight down, so it moves along the beach in a sawtooth pattern.

items.prompt: How far can beach sand travel along the shore in a single day through this swash-and-backwash zigzag?

options.label: A few millimeters
A few centimeters
Many tens of meters
Dozens of kilometers

items.explain: On days with oblique wind, beach sand can move downbeach in a sawtooth fashion many tens of meters per day.

items.prompt: Two beaches face the same sea, but sediment on one heads north and on the other heads south. What most likely sets the direction?

options.label: The height of the tides on each beach
The angle at which the waves arrive
The temperature of the water offshore
The depth of the ocean far out at sea

items.explain: Longshore drift depends on the angle of incoming waves; early 20th-century researchers found that angle to be of paramount importance.

items.prompt: Shingle beaches are much steeper than sandy ones, so waves tend to plunge rather than roll in. Where does most of the sideways transport happen there?

options.label: Far offshore, beyond the breakers
In the dunes behind the beach
On the deep sea floor past the shelf
Where water rushes up the beach face

items.explain: With plunging breakers and no wide surf zone, most longshore transport on shingle beaches happens in the swash zone.

items.prompt: A long beach faces the same prevailing wind and waves year after year. What pattern does the idea of a drift-aligned beach predict?

options.label: Sand spreads evenly along the whole length
Sand builds up on one side as the other erodes
The whole beach erodes at the same rate
The beach stays fixed once it has formed

items.explain: A drift-aligned beach forms from prevailing wind and wave directions, with deposition on one side and erosion on the other.

items.prompt: Sand drifting along a coast reaches a tidal inlet with shoals on its seaward side. What do those shoals do with the sand?

options.label: Grind it into fine mud that washes away
Trap it for good so no sand passes
Store it and can pass it on to other beaches
Push it inland up the river channel

items.explain: Ebb-tidal shoals at inlets store sand brought by longshore transport and may also pass it on to other beach systems.

paragraphs.heading: What longshore drift is
paragraphs.text: Longshore drift is the movement of sediment along a coast, running parallel to the shore. The material can be clay, silt, sand, pebbles, shingle or shells. It is carried by a longshore current, and the drift is simply the sediment that this current moves. Both the current and the moving sediment stay within the surf zone. Another name for the process is littoral drift.

paragraphs.heading: It all depends on the angle
paragraphs.text: The angle at which waves arrive decides how the drift behaves. When wind comes in at a slant, it pushes water sideways along the coast and sets up a current that runs parallel to the shore. Scientists came to see the angle of wave approach as crucial for moving sediment, and longshore currents as the main force carrying it along the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Sand that zigzags
paragraphs.text: Sand on the beach itself also moves on these slanting-wind days. A breaking wave runs up the beach at an angle, which is called the swash, and gravity then drains the water straight back down the slope, at right angles to the shore, which is called the backwash. The result is a sawtooth path, and sand can travel along the beach many tens of meters in a day. This is called beach drift, though some researchers count it as part of longshore drift, since the overall effect is sand moving along the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Sand beaches and shingle beaches
paragraphs.text: Drift works a little differently depending on the size of the sediment, so a sandy beach and a shingle beach do not behave the same way. Sand is moved mostly by the back-and-forth push of breaking waves, by the impact of those waves, and by the drag of the longshore current on the bed. Shingle beaches are much steeper, so plunging breakers are more likely there. Without a wide surf zone, most of the movement on a shingle beach happens in the swash zone.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea developed
paragraphs.text: People knew in ancient times that coasts erode and sediment moves, especially where shores change dramatically, but those early accounts were mostly anecdotal. Fishermen, sailors and locals saw sand and gravel apparently travelling down beaches without understanding why. Systematic study began in the mid-1800s, with early theories from the French engineer Jean-Baptiste Fourier and the Irish geologist Robert Mallet. They studied waves and sediment before the term longshore drift had even been coined. In the early 20th century, oceanographers and coastal engineers sharpened the explanation a great deal.

paragraphs.heading: Beaches shaped by drift
paragraphs.text: One idea from that period was the drift-aligned beach: a beach shaped by the prevailing wind and wave directions, with sand building up at one side and wearing away at the other. Sand moved by drift can also be stored for a while. Ebb-tidal shoals at inlets hold sand delivered by longshore transport and can pass it on to other beaches. That makes them both sources and sinks in a coast's sediment budget.
